client: Lately, I’ve been feeling really empty and disconnected from everything. Ever since my dad passed away two months ago, it’s like I can’t find joy in things I used to enjoy, and I feel like my friends don’t really understand what I’m going through. I guess I’m just not sure if talking about it here will actually help me feel better.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of grief and loneliness since your dad’s passing, and it’s understandable that you’re feeling disconnected from things that once brought you joy. It’s okay to feel unsure about whether talking here will help—what’s coming up for you as you share this with me now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I feel kind of relieved to say it out loud, but also a little overwhelmed. It’s like, I know I need to process it, but I’m scared of getting stuck in the sadness. I also worry that people expect me to just “move on” already, and that makes me feel even more alone.
therapist: It sounds like sharing this brought up a mix of relief and overwhelm, and it’s understandable to feel hesitant about diving into the sadness while also sensing pressure to “move on.” It’s okay to take this at your own pace—what do you think might help you feel less alone in this process?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know... maybe talking to people who've actually lost a parent? But then I think, why would they want to listen to my pain when they're dealing with their own? It feels selfish to reach out, even though part of me really needs that connection.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between needing connection and fearing it might burden others—that’s such a difficult conflict to hold. The way your voice softened as you said this makes me wonder if part of you is carrying guilt for needing support—would you say that feels true?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I do feel guilty. Like, I shouldn’t need so much help or take up so much space with my grief. I keep thinking, “Shouldn’t I be stronger than this?” But then I also feel like I’m drowning, and I don’t know how to get out of it. It’s just... confusing.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a lot of tension between feeling like you *should* be stronger and the very real, overwhelming weight of your grief. That confusion makes so much sense—grief doesn’t follow a rulebook, and it’s okay to need support, even if it feels uncomfortable. What would it be like to give yourself permission to take up space with your feelings, without judgment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Giving myself permission feels... impossible right now. It’s like I’ve built this wall around my grief, and if I let myself take up space with it, I’m scared it’ll just swallow me whole. I don’t know how to do that without feeling like I’m falling apart.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a part of you that’s holding back—almost as if your words are saying one thing, but your tone feels a bit lighter, like there’s a flicker of hope or energy beneath the fear. What do you think might be keeping that wall in place, even as part of you seems ready to explore what’s on the other side?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think the wall is there because I’m scared of losing control. If I let myself really feel the grief, I worry I’ll never be able to pull myself back together. It’s like I’m holding onto this idea that I need to stay strong, even though I know deep down that’s not helping me heal.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying this fear that if you let go, even a little, everything might unravel—that’s such a heavy burden to hold. But I also hear something important in what you’re saying: the awareness that staying “strong” might not actually be helping you heal. What do you think would happen if you let yourself loosen that grip, just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I don't know... maybe I'd finally start to process things? But it's terrifying to think about. Like what if I start crying and can't stop? Or what if people see me differently if I'm not holding it together all the time? I've been the "strong one" in my family for so long.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a lot of fear tied to letting go of that “strong one” role—like you’re worried about what might happen if you show vulnerability, both for yourself and how others might see you. What do you think it would mean for you to take small steps toward processing this grief, even if it feels scary?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: Small steps feel... manageable, I guess. But I’m still scared of what might come up. Like, what if I start crying and can’t stop? Or what if I let myself feel it and it’s worse than I imagined? I’m not sure I’m ready to face that yet.
therapist: It sounds like you’re open to the idea of small steps, but there’s still a lot of fear about what might come up if you let yourself feel the grief more fully. That fear is completely valid—it’s a big step to trust yourself with those emotions. What do you think might help you feel safer to take that first small step, even if it’s just a tiny one?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Maybe if I had someone to check in with after I let myself feel a little bit of it—like, someone who could help me feel grounded afterward. But I’m still worried I’ll just spiral and won’t be able to handle it on my own. It feels like such a risk.
therapist: It sounds like having someone to check in with afterward could help you feel more grounded and supported as you start to explore those feelings. That worry about spiraling is so understandable—it’s a big step to trust yourself with emotions that feel overwhelming. What might it look like to have a small, safe way to dip your toes into those feelings, knowing you have support afterward?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think maybe I could try journaling for just five minutes about how I’m feeling, and then text a friend afterward to check in. But I’m still nervous—what if writing makes me feel worse, and then I’m stuck with those feelings? It’s hard to trust that I’ll be okay afterward.
therapist: It sounds like journaling for a short time and then checking in with a friend could be a gentle way to start exploring your feelings while still feeling supported. It’s completely normal to feel nervous about what might come up—what do you think might help you feel a little more secure in trusting yourself through this process?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
